children: By Margherita Stancati and Marcos García Rey
MADRID — Hours after the death of an elderly woman known as Maricarmen in Madrid, the political jockeying over her legacy had already begun.

María del Carmen Abascal, 87, died in a hospital two weeks after she was forcibly evicted from a flat where she had lived for decades. Televised scenes of her being carried away from the flat on a stretcher sparked nationwide protests against Spain's housing crisis.

Abascal had become the face of the struggle to fix Spain's broken housing market — the top concern for Spaniards ahead of general elections on Nov. 29. Her death on Wednesday, days after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced the election, reshaped her story, turning her into a political martyr, as the country enters election mode.

As grief gives way to anger, the question is which candidate is best equipped to convince Spaniards that they can prevent what happened to Abascal from happening again. Politicians across the spectrum weighed in on her death almost immediately.
Sánchez extended his condolences to Abascal's loved ones and sent "a hug to everyone who today feels this loss as our own."

"Maricarmen did not die, she was murdered by the vultures who wanted to take her house, the justice system and the administrations that allowed it," said Ione Belarra, the leader of the far-left Podemos party, using a code word for real estate and investment firms.

"They have killed Maricarmen," the far-right Vox party said on its official X account. "They have used the suffering of an elderly person to stage a campaign that hides the Government's responsibility in the housing disaster." The party blamed the housing crisis on migrant arrivals under Sánchez.

Opinion polls show the left-wing Sánchez is heading for electoral defeat against the conservative People's Party, which would likely enter a coalition with Vox if it wins. Sánchez and his allies see housing as a social justice issue that might turn their fortunes around.
The stakes are high, and Abascal's story is bound to remain central to election campaigns, said Beatriz Becerra, a political analyst and a former centrist lawmaker at the European Parliament.

"Attempts to turn a person's death into an electoral weapon are concerning, and I am concerned about this happening on both sides," she said. "The best tribute to Maricarmen is to ensure that, once the campaigns end, something changes in the conditions that made her eviction possible."

Housing wasn't a major issue in Spain until recently. Now, nearly 90% of Spaniards consider it a political priority, according to a poll published this week by Spain's state-run Center for Sociological Studies.

Spain has a shortage of more than 700,000 homes, according to the country's central bank. Immigration, tourism and urban concentration have driven up demand. Meanwhile, bureaucratic delays, strict construction rules and rent control in cities such as Barcelona have crimped supply, sending property prices and rents skyrocketing.

The Spanish government earlier this week introduced a series of measures aimed at tackling the crisis, including extending a ban on evictions and providing tax breaks for tenants and small property owners.

Sánchez, who has been in power for more than eight years, could have done more to address the housing crisis much earlier on, said Diego Sánchez de la Cruz, an economic analyst at the Juan de Mariana Institute, a libertarian think tank.

"When you see an 87-year-old being evicted from her home 99.9% of people react negatively, everyone shows solidarity. But this case is more complicated," said de la Cruz. "We should not kick someone out on the street. But you cannot impose this cost, this housing cost, on property owners."
Abascal's story begins in 1956, during the military dictatorship of Francisco Franco, when her father signed a rent-controlled lease on a flat in Madrid's now-affluent El Retiro neighborhood.

Abascal, who lived alone since her mother died in 2005, eventually inherited the lease. Although it expired in 2007, the owners allowed her to stay, paying roughly EUR500 monthly — worth $560 — in rent and utilities, according to court documents and public statements.
In 2018, a real-estate investment firm called Urbagestión bought her apartment. For two years, her rent arrangement was unchanged.
Then Urbagestión raised the rent to a level more in line with market prices, but Abascal couldn't afford it on her EUR1,450 monthly pension.

Abascal fought legally to keep her home. Spain's highest court in 2023 ruled in favor of Urbagestión. Six unsuccessful eviction attempts followed as Abascal spoke publicly of her plight and in defense of other vulnerable tenants.

She blamed the Spanish government for failing to protect people like her. She appealed directly to Sánchez in an open letter last year: "You have the ability, the responsibility, and the power to change this," she wrote. "This house is mine, not because I bought it, but because I've lived in it."
She added: "Mr. President, when your term ends, I would like to still be here, in the same place where I was the day you were born." She never heard back.

Abascal, who had limited mobility and other health issues, was carried away from her apartment on a stretcher on Sept. 23 to a Madrid hospital. Mass protests followed. Under pressure from the public, Urbagestión agreed to have Abascal return to her flat at low rent once discharged from the hospital.
She died before setting foot in it again.
